summary: This memo is an official ICCB and DARPA policy statement on rolling out the Exterior Gateway Protocol. After 1 August 1984 every gateway had to belong to an autonomous system, and some gateway of each system had to exchange routing information with the core using EGP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 890 sets a timetable for replacing gateways that did not share routing information dynamically. It says each gateway must join an autonomous system and that each system must exchange routing information with the core using EGP.

subtitle: A policy timetable for replacing dumb gateways with EGP-capable gateways.

tldr.problem: Gateways that did not exchange routing information dynamically had to be entered and updated manually in other gateways' tables.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out a staged transition: add stub EGP support, organize gateways into autonomous systems, and then use full EGP between systems.
tldr.outcome: The policy required every Internet gateway to belong to an autonomous system after 1 August 1984 and each system to exchange routes with the core using EGP.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 890's status as Unknown. The memo identifies itself as an official ICCB and DARPA policy statement for EGP implementation.

sections.title: Why the Gateway Setup Needed to Change
sections.content:
Smart gateways exchanged routing information with one another using the Gateway Gateway Protocol. Dumb gateways did not exchange routing information dynamically, so smart gateways needed manually maintained entries for them.

The memo says existing GGP procedures were near their capacity and that a significant change was needed. Stub gateways connected a single network at the edge of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Some gateways shared routes automatically, while others depended on manual entries. The memo says the existing arrangement was running near its limits.

sections.title: A Three-Step Transition
sections.content:
The first step was to replace dumb gateways with gateways that implement at least the Stub Exterior Gateway Protocol, described in RFC 888. The next step was to group gateways into autonomous systems, with smaller systems attached to a larger core system using EGP.

The final step was to specify full EGP and allow richer connections among autonomous systems. Each system could use its own internal routing procedures as long as participating gateways communicated with other systems through EGP.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan first adds basic EGP support, then groups gateways into systems, and finally allows broader routing exchanges between those systems.

sections.title: The Gateway Policy Deadline
sections.content:
The policy states that after 1 August 1984 there would be no dumb gateways in the Internet. Every gateway had to belong to an autonomous system, and at least one gateway in each system had to exchange routing information with a gateway in the core system using EGP.

The memo tells operators with a dumb gateway to begin upgrading or replacing it. It also lists groups working on EGP gateways and describes testing and contact arrangements.
sections.plainLanguage: After the stated deadline, every gateway had to be part of a system using EGP to exchange routes with the core. The memo directs operators to upgrade or replace gateways that did not meet the policy.
